prompt: Write an email to a colleague about the first week of planting a vegetable garden. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the email only.
final_message:
Subject: Week one in the vegetable garden

Dear Marcus,

You asked how the garden was coming along, and I am pleased to report that nothing has died yet; I am told this is the correct benchmark for the first week.

I began on Saturday with the turf, which did not wish to leave. I removed a plot roughly ten feet by twelve, and the turf resisted with a tenacity I had not seen since the last budget meeting. I will admit that it took most of the morning, and that my back has filed a formal complaint. Having dug out the grass, I turned the soil over and worked in a few barrows of compost. The soil is darker than I expected, which I choose to credit to my own character rather than to the previous owner's habits.

On Sunday I planted. In went the peas along the north fence, where they can climb without shading anything else; two short rows of lettuce; some radishes, because they are said to come up quickly and a man in my position needs early encouragement; and a double row of carrots, which I sowed thinly and then thinned again out of pure nerves. The tomatoes and zucchini I have kept indoors on the windowsill, as the nights are still cold enough to be unreasonable. The zucchini, I am warned, will in due course produce more than any household can eat, and I am already composing the notes to the neighbors.

The week since has been given over to watering and watching. I have stood at the edge of the bed more often than the situation strictly requires. Nothing has happened; this is, I gather, how seeds work. On Thursday I thought I saw a radish, but on closer inspection it was a pebble. I have marked every row with a stake and a label, partly for order and partly so that I can tell the carrots from the weeds when the weeds arrive, as they surely will.

I did buy a proper hoe, with a long handle and a sharp blade. It lets one work standing upright, like a reasonable person, and I recommend it. If you are still thinking about a bed of your own, I will gladly lend it to you, along with any opinions you did not ask for.

I will report again when something has actually come up. Do come by on Saturday if you are free; there is nothing to see yet, but the coffee is decent.

Walter
